elements.content: Grammar focus: Inversion after Negative Adverbials.

Front the negative adverbial, find the auxiliary the sentence needs, then invert. If the clause has no auxiliary, add do, does or did and use the base verb. Keep no sooner ... than together, and never invert the second clause.

never / rarely / seldom — invert with the existing auxiliary: rarely has the board been so divided
not only ... but also — invert the first clause only: not only did costs rise, but quality fell
not until / only when — invert the main clause: not until June did the figures appear
under no circumstances / on no account — invert the modal: under no circumstances should the data be shared
no sooner ... than — invert the first clause, than in the second: no sooner had we signed than the price fell
hardly ... when — invert the first clause, when in the second: hardly had we started when the line stopped
Guided practice: choose the correct option.
1. Complete: 'Rarely ___ such a divided vote.'
2. Complete: 'No sooner ___ than the price fell.'
3. Which clause inverts in 'not only ... but also'?
Read and listen: three examples in context.

Rarely has the board been so divided. — The board has rarely been so divided. (Fronted rare + inversion.)
Not until June did the figures appear. — The figures did not appear until June. (Not until + inversion.)
No sooner had we signed than the price fell. — We had no sooner signed than the price fell. (No sooner ... than.)
What do you observe?

When a negative or limiting adverbial opens the clause, the subject and auxiliary swap. The auxiliary is the one the sentence already needs: have for a perfect, did for a past simple, should or will for a modal. With no sooner and hardly, the second clause takes than or when, and it does not invert.
1. What moves in an inverted clause?
options: The main verb and the object.

elements.content: 2. Which word follows 'no sooner' in the second clause?

Freer production: Can deliver dramatic rhetorical emphasis in formal presentations and economic briefings using negative inversion

Success criteria:
- I can invert after never, rarely and seldom.
- I can use not only ... but also with the auxiliary in the right place.
- I can keep no sooner ... than and hardly ... when intact.
Role play: put your position in ninety seconds; your partner notes every use of the target structure.
Frequent errors and correction:

❌ Never I have seen such a decline (no inversion after a fronted negative) → ✅ Never have I seen such a decline
❌ Not only costs rose, but quality fell (missing auxiliary in the first clause) → ✅ Not only did costs rise, but quality fell
Correct these sentences: say what is wrong, then give the right version.
Acceptable variants:

Not until the audit closed did the scale of the loss emerge.
Only if the fee is paid will the application proceed.
No sooner had the vote ended than the resignations began.
